programs.name: Elderly Exemption Property Tax Credit
programs._raw:
{
  "name": "Elderly Exemption Property Tax Credit",
  "eligibility": {
    "age": 65,
    "income_limits": "This is a local-option New Hampshire elderly property tax exemption, so the income limits, exemption amount, and sometimes the age-band thresholds are set by each city or town. State law only sets minimums: for the elderly exemption, a municipality must allow at least $13,400 net income for a single applicant and $20,400 combined net income for a married couple, and many towns set much higher local limits. Some municipalities publish their own limits, such as single $40,000 / married $57,000 in Rochester, single $50,000 / married or civil union $60,000 in Hudson, and single $50,000 / married $65,000 in North Hampton. Because this varies by municipality, the family must check the applicant’s town/city assessing office for the exact current limit.",
    "asset_limits": "State law requires a net asset limit of at least $35,000 excluding the value of the residence; municipalities may set a higher limit. In some towns, the principal residence is excluded from assets, and some local guides explicitly exclude it while counting other net assets. The exact asset cap and what counts can vary locally, so check the town/city form or worksheet. Commonly counted assets include non-residence net assets; the home itself is excluded from the asset test in many municipalities.",
    "other_requirements": [
      "Applicant must be a New Hampshire resident for at least 3 consecutive years before April 1 of the tax year.",
      "Applicant must own the property individually or jointly, or the spouse must own it.",
      "The property must be the applicant’s principal residence / permanent place of abode.",
      "If married, the couple must have been married for at least 5 consecutive years before April 1.",
      "Applicant must meet the municipality’s income and asset limits.",
      "Age bands are local, but state law allows age categories starting at 65 and requires at least one exemption category for ages 65+, 75+, and 80+; many towns use 65–74, 75–79, and 80+."
    ]
  },
  "benefits": {
    "type": "financial",
    "value": "This is a property tax exemption, meaning a dollar amount is deducted from the assessed value of the home before property taxes are calculated. The amount varies by municipality and age band. Examples include Exeter: $152,251 off assessed value (65–74), $183,751 (75–79), $236,251 (80+); Salem: $156,000, $234,000, $318,500; Manchester: $156,000, $210,000, $280,000; Hudson: $132,000, $156,000, $233,000; Dover: $206,000, $291,000, $373,000.",
    "varies_by": "household_size"
  },
  "application": {
    "methods": [
      "In person at the local assessing/tax assessor office",
      "By mail, where the municipality allows mailed submission",
      "Sometimes by appointment with the assessor’s office"
    ],
    "processing_time": "Typically handled on the local tax-year filing schedule, with filing deadlines often around April 1 or April 15 depending on the town. No statewide processing-time standard was identified; review timing is municipal and tied to the tax assessment calendar.",
    "waitlist": null,
    "forms": [
      "Form PA-29, Permanent Application for Property Tax Credit/Exemptions",
      "Municipal Elderly Exemption Worksheet / Qualification Worksheet",
      "If property is held in trust, Form PA-33, Statement of Qualification"
    ],
    "documents": [
      "Completed PA-29",
      "Municipal elderly exemption worksheet or qualification worksheet",
      "Proof of age",
      "Proof of New Hampshire residency for 3 years",
      "Deed or proof of ownership",
      "Marriage documentation if qualifying through a spouse",
      "Income documentation for the prior year or applicable filing year",
      "Asset information for non-residence assets",
      "Trust documents if the property is held in trust"
    ]
  },
  "geography": {
    "statewide": true,
    "restrictions": "Available only in municipalities that adopt the elderly exemption under New Hampshire law; the program is local-option, not automatic statewide uniformity.",
    "regional_variations": "Yes. Each city or town can set its own exemption dollar amounts, income limits above the state minimum, asset limits above the state minimum, filing deadlines, and sometimes its own worksheet or affidavit. Wait times and appointment requirements also vary by municipality.",
    "offices_or_providers": [
      "Local town/city assessing office",
      "Local tax assessor office",
      "Selectmen’s office in some towns for form pickup or filing assistance"
    ]
  },
  "official_source": "https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/v/72/72-39-b.htm",
  "gotchas": [
    "This is not a state-uniform benefit; the exact dollar amounts change by municipality.",
    "People often confuse the exemption with a tax credit: it usually lowers assessed value, not the tax bill by a fixed credit amount.",
    "The filing deadline is local and may be earlier than the tax bill due date.",
    "Some towns require a separate elderly qualification worksheet in addition to PA-29.",
    "If the home is in a trust, extra paperwork may be required.",
    "Spouses’ ownership and marriage-duration rules can affect eligibility even if only one spouse is the applicant.",
    "The residence is often excluded from asset limits, but other assets are not.",
    "Income definitions can vary slightly by municipality, so applicants should verify whether Social Security and other income sources are counted."
  ],
  "data_shape_notes": "This program is a local-option property tax exemption with municipality-specific dollar amounts, income caps, asset caps, and deadlines. The core structure is fixed statewide, but the actual numbers and forms vary by town or city.",
}
